title: Atopic eczema | NHS inform
text:
Atopic eczema
Atopic eczema (atopic dermatitis) is a common skin condition that causes itchy skin. It can affect anyone, but it’s most common in children. Atopic eczema is a long term condition but can improve over time.
Symptoms of atopic eczema
Atopic eczema can happen anywhere but it’s most common on the hands, elbows and knees. It’s common on the face and scalp in children.
Atopic eczema can make your skin:
itchy
dry, cracked, crusty, scaly or thickened
red, white, purple or grey
lighter or darker than the skin around it (depending on your skin tone)
blister or bleed
painful
The severity of atopic eczema can vary from person to person. There may also be times when your symptoms get worse (a flare-up) and times when they improve.
Atopic eczema can cause areas of pink, raised skin.
Babies and children often have atopic eczema symptoms on their face.
Speak to your GP practice immediately or phone 111 if:
You or your child have atopic eczema and:
it’s blistered, crusty, leaking fluid or has spots filled with pus
it’s painful, swollen or feels warm
it suddenly gets worse or gets bigger
have a high temperature or feel generally unwell
Speak to your GP practice if:
you or your child have symptoms of atopic eczema
treatments are not helping your atopic eczema
Diagnosing atopic eczema
Your GP will look at your skin and ask questions about your symptoms to help diagnose atopic eczema. For example, they may ask when the symptoms began, whether they come and go and if you have a family history of eczema.
If you have severe atopic eczema, your GP may refer you to a skin specialist (dermatologist).
Getting advice from a pharmacist
A pharmacist can give you advice about atopic eczema if your symptoms are mild. For example, you have small areas of dry or slightly itchy skin. If your symptoms are more severe, speak to your GP.
Find your nearest pharmacy
Treatment for atopic eczema
There’s no cure for atopic eczema but treatments can help improve symptoms.
The main treatments for atopic eczema are:
moisturising creams, lotions, ointments and gels that you apply to your skin
steroid creams, lotions or gels that you apply to your skin (topical corticosteroids)
Special dressings or medicines may help to treat more severe atopic eczema symptoms.
Things you can do to help atopic eczema
There are some things you can do to help your atopic eczema symptoms.
Do
apply moisturising treatments (emollients) to your skin as often as possible
continue to moisturise even if your eczema improves
wash with an emollient instead of soap
keep your nails short and clean to reduce damage to your skin
put anti-scratch mittens on babies to stop them scratching their skin
wear soft, light clothing
keep cool – heat can make eczema symptoms worse
Don’t
do not scratch the skin as it can make your symptoms worse
–
try gently rubbing your skin with your fingers
do not use soaps and detergents that irritate your skin
do not share emollients with other people
do not put your fingers into an emollient pot – use a spoon or pump dispenser instead
do not use aqueous cream as it can irritate the skin and make eczema worse
do not change your diet unless you’re told to by a doctor
What causes atopic eczema?
It’s not always clear what causes atopic eczema.
You may be more likely to get atopic eczema if:
one or both of your parents have atopic eczema
you or a close family member have an allergy like
asthma
or
hayfever
Some things can also make atopic eczema worse, including:
allergens
–
like soap, detergent, pets, pollen or some foods
heat
changes in temperature
stress
some types of clothing
–
like those made from wool or synthetic fibres
hormonal changes – for example, during
pregnancy
or
menopause
skin infections
Atopic eczema is not infectious so it can’t be passed on to others.
Complications of atopic eczema
Atopic eczema can cause the skin to become cracked and broken. This can sometimes lead to infections. You should see your doctor as soon as possible if you think you or your child’s skin may have become infected.
Having itchy skin caused by atopic eczema can disrupt your sleep. This may cause tiredness and difficulty concentrating during the day.
Living with atopic eczema can be difficult. If it’s affecting your mental health, you may be referred to a mental health specialist.
